articles.title: No pillars, extra floors, 'illegal' repair work: What brought down a 4-decade-old PG in Satya Niketan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A waterlogged basement, repair work on an ageing structure and possible structural weaknesses are emerging as key factors behind the deadly.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A waterlogged basement, repair work on an ageing structure and possible structural weaknesses are emerging as key factors behind the deadly collapse of a student PG building in Delhi's Satya Niketan.As cops piece together what caused the decades-old structure to come down, eyewitness accounts and preliminary official findings have pointed to a potentially dangerous combination of accumulated water, ongoing construction activity and floors added over the years.Chief minister Rekha Gupta said the building was a very old structure. The ongoing repair work, combined with the accumulated water, led to the collapse, she said after inspecting the site.Police, meanwhile, said renovation work was allegedly being carried out on the ground floor and in the basement before the building collapsed. An FIR has been registered against the alleged owner and others, while investigators examine who was responsible and whether the repair work compromised the structure.The building, which was more than four decades old, was being used as a paying guest accommodation for students. MCD officials are also examining whether recent heavy rain and seepage weakened the structure.The civic body has said it is still too early to establish the exact cause, with investigators looking into the possible role of water seepage, basement or ground-floor work, and the building's structural condition.Eyewitness accounts from the site have added another layer to the questions surrounding the collapse. A local resident said the building was part of an old cluster in Satya Niketan where structures were originally constructed decades ago and additional floors were later added.“The building had no pillars. In the Satya Niketan area, many houses do not have pillars. These are old buildings, constructed when Satya Niketan was first developed, and floors have since been added to these structures. In the building that collapsed, some work was on in the basement. Water had accumulated there,” the resident said.Former Delhi Fire Services director Atul Garg also pointed to two major factors that can commonly trigger the collapse of an old building — heavy rain and construction activity. According to him, both factors were present in the Satya Niketan case, making the structure particularly vulnerable.The collapse itself was so sudden and violent that many residents initially believed an earthquake had struck.“We felt the ground shake. When we ran outside, we saw that a house had completely collapsed,” said Roshan Pal, a student from Lucknow.Another resident, Rahul Gaur, said a massive cloud of dust engulfed the area moments after the structure came down. “When I came out, a cloud of dust was spreading in all directions. That’s when we realised that the building had collapsed,” he said.As screams for help came from beneath the rubble, students and local residents began the first rescue efforts even before heavy machinery could be deployed. Witnesses said those trapped inside shouted “bachao, bachao humein” as residents formed human chains to clear debris.Some locals arranged oxygen cylinders and tried to pump oxygen through gaps in the rubble to help those trapped breathe. Students and residents manually removed smaller pieces of concrete and created pathways through the debris to prevent rescue operations from slowing down.Delhi University was also trying to determine how many of its students were living in the building. South Campus director Professor Rajni Abbi said colleges had been asked to assess the number of students residing in Satya Niketan and ensure their safety.Student organisations, including volunteers from ABVP, NSUI and AISA, also joined the early rescue efforts. DUSU president Aryan Maan said he reached the site within minutes and mobilised student volunteers from South Campus to help dig through the rubble and evacuate survivors.Questions have also been raised over the building's construction history and its conversion for commercial use. Garg said the structure was originally built for residential purposes and was later expanded with additional floors, raising concerns about whether its structural strength was adequate.The tragedy has now put the spotlight on Delhi's ageing buildings, particularly residential structures being used as PGs and other commercial establishments. The Delhi government has announced plans for mandatory periodic structural audits and safety certification for old buildings being used by the public.The exact cause of the collapse, however, will be established only after the magisterial inquiry and the ongoing police and civic investigations are completed.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Watch: Deadly pyrotechnic explosion rocks church festival in Mexico, 10 killed
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A celebration turned tragedy in Mexico killed at least 10 people while leaving 64 injured after pyrotechnic material exploded during a religious festi.
articles.body: A celebration turned tragedy in Mexico killed at least 10 people while leaving 64 injured after pyrotechnic material exploded during a religious festival in Temascalcingo on Saturday night. The explosion collapsed walls and sent hundreds of people fleeing in panic, authorities said.The blast occurred beside the Nuestra Señora de la Luz church in the central Mexican town where residents were gathered to watch a fireworks display being held as part of celebrations for the local patron saint. The municipality is located about 160 kilometres (100 miles) northwest of Mexico City.The explosion brought down the walls of surrounding buildings and triggered a fire in the town square.Footage circulating online from the accident shows people dancing around with the firework structure in celebration. It was after a couple of rounds that the pyrotechnics began going berserk. Due to the nature of the structure, the smoke from the firework billowed rapidly in the air before the people could react to the mishap.Videos from the aftermath were also circulated online showing people moving through thick smoke and scattered debris as they searched for survivors. Some victims were reportedly trapped beneath collapsed structures.The cause of the explosion has not yet been established. The Mexico State Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation into the incident.A local bishop said two priests were among those injured in the blast.The explosion occurred during a traditional festival ritual in which a straw bull fitted with fireworks is burned and carried around the town. Video footage showed the blast striking as crowds stood outside the church, with the force of the explosion causing widespread panic.Emergency responders and residents rushed to help those caught in the blast, as the scale of the destruction became clear in the aftermath.Temascalcingo, a municipality with about 66,000 residents, was hosting hundreds of people for the religious celebrations when the explosion occurred.The incident has once again highlighted the dangers posed by pyrotechnics in Mexico, where fireworks are widely used during street celebrations, religious festivals and other public gatherings.Similar accidents have occurred in the country before. Nearly four years ago, a powerful fireworks explosion in a village in the municipality of Huejutla, in the central state of Hidalgo, left 17 people injured.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bus fares in west of Scotland now capped at £2 - but some call it 'half a solution'
articles.summary: The SNP policy was announced last week and from Monday, fares are capped to £2 in the west.
articles.body:
The Scottish government's policy to cap bus fares in the west of Scotland at £2 has taken effect.

First Minister John Swinney announced the move as part of his programme for government last week.

From Monday, the £2 trips are being offered in Glasgow, Renfrewshire, Ayrshire, Dunbartonshire, Lanarkshire and Inverclyde - part of a promise to cap fares across the whole of Scotland by the end of the parliamentary term.

A pilot of the scheme has already been rolled out in the Highlands and islands, but Swinney has not said when it would be extended to the rest of the country.

The fare cap in Strathclyde is operating in 12 local authority areas:

Twenty five bus operators are currently participating in the Strathclyde scheme, with additional companies expected to join in the coming weeks.

The Scottish government has invested £10m in the pilot, which has been tested in the Highlands , Western Isles , Orkney , Shetland Moray , and Argyll and Bute for the past year.

As it extends to the west of the country, participating bus operators will be reimbursed by public body Transport Scotland.

Swinney said bus travel was the most widely used form of public transport in Scotland and the government was working to make it "as affordable, accessible and attractive as possible".

He said: "This is vital to grow the economy, travel sustainably and protect the planet."

First Bus, one of the bigger bus companies operating across Glasgow, Dumbarton, Kirkintilloch and Lanarkshire, said it would continue to work with the government to ensure the cap was a success.

But just days before the start of the scheme, another bus company expressed concern over how it would work across non-participating areas.

Electric bus company Ember called the £2 cap "a good slogan" but raised concerns about the way the Scottish government funds the scheme.

A spokesperson said: "In essence, we are strongly supportive of the goals of the scheme and of the underpinning principles of better bus travel. Our concern is around the mechanism proposed to achieve this."

Paul White, director at Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT) Scotland, told BBC Scotland that most operators were ready.

"Our larger members are prepared to go live on Monday morning but CPT doesn't represent every single bus operator in the Strathclyde area."

He said there was a lot to pull together in a short space of time.

"We had to understand the scope of the scheme, how reimbursement would work, how operators will be paid for carrying these services and meeting the gov's commitment," he said.

Ticket machines had to be updated and back office administration put in place.

He also said that operators have to be able to make sure the £2 scheme is not going to harm the bus network.

A similar £2 cap in England resulted in a 5% rise in bus use, he said.

"There are potential unintended consequences such as the number of additional passengers being greater than the current network can cope with.

"Dwell times is another - more passengers boarding the bus and telling the driver where they are going - that can increase boarding times that will increase journey times for other passengers."

He added: "The £2 fare cap is an eye-catching initiative that should help attract passengers and help existing passengers manage the cost of living.

"But a fares-only approach to bus support is inadequate. We really need steps to make buses more reliable, free them from congestion and we need a multi-year commitment to funding bus priority to go alongside schemes such as the £2 fare cap."

Campaigner Ellie Harrison agrees that there is more to be done although this is a good start.

She said the £2 scheme was just a partial solution.

"The fare cap is only going to address half the problem with the deregulation of bus services," she said. "It is going to do nothing to improve the quality of services."

She went on: "It's going to do nothing to put on new routes to communities who have been cut off by private bus companies cancelling services over the past few decades.

"And it is going to do nothing to integrate our bus network with the other transport modes - the subway, train and active travel.

"The only way we can achieve that is by supporting our transport authority SPT - Strathclyde Partnership for Transport - to progress its plans to bring the bus network into public control."

Transport Scotland said it had engaged closely with bus operators and participation in the scheme was voluntary.

A spokesperson said: "The cost of living remains one of the biggest challenges facing households across Scotland, which is why making public transport more affordable through the £2 bus fare cap is such an important priority for the Scottish government."

articles.title: Republican Mayor of American city on Lake Ontario' shore rejects the name change to 'Lake America' that Google and Apple have adopted; says: My community …
articles.summary: Tech News News: The Republican mayor of Oswego, New York, Robert Corradino, has rejected the renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a change enacted by US Presid.
articles.body: The Republican mayor of Oswego, New York, Robert Corradino, has rejected the renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a change enacted by US President Donald Trump through an executive order on August 27. While Google and Apple Maps have already adopted the new name for US users, Corradino said his community is “taking the renaming very personally” and will continue to use Lake Ontario in all signage, tourism materials, and official communications. According to a report by National Post, Corradino emphasized that Lake Ontario is central to Oswego’s identity, citing its economic importance through charter boats, cruise ships, and tourism.The renaming of ‘Lake Ontario’ and local pushbackCorradino emphasized that Lake Ontario's name is rooted in a Huron Indigenous word meaning "lake of shining waters," predating the province of Ontario itself, which took its name from the lake in 1867. “Lake Ontario is in the DNA of Osweganians. Everything that we are emanates from the lake,” he said. The mayor also noted that Canadian tourism, vital to local businesses, has dropped substantially following the breakdown of US-Canada trade negotiations last month. Statistics Canada data shows Canadian travel to the US fell 10.6% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.Corradino reaffirmed Oswego’s stance: “Lake Ontario has carried its name for hundreds of years. It is a name rooted in history, geography, and the shared identity of the communities that surround it. The city of Oswego will continue using the name that reflects our history and honors the generations who have lived, worked, and built their lives along its shores.”A Bipartisan and cross-border backlashTrump's order has drawn criticism well beyond Oswego. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton responded to the renaming with a brief rebuttal on X, while Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders said the American public has no appetite for calling the lake "Lake America."North of the border, Carney noted on social media that the name Lake Ontario derives from the Wendat word "Ontari'io," meaning the lake is beautiful and big, and that it predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence by more than 400 years. He argued that acknowledging reality means continuing to call it Lake Ontario. Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre echoed the sentiment, saying the lake was never Trump's to rename on a whim.Ontario Premier Doug Ford went a step further on Saturday, unveiling a new "Lake Ontario" sign in Winona, Ontario, declaring in a video posted to X that the lake carried that name long before Trump and would continue to carry it long after he's gone.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Since 2007, New York's Rockefeller Center Christmas tree has been milled into lumber after the holidays; the wood has helped build Habitat homes from New York to Mississippi
articles.summary: US News: For millions of people, the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree is a familiar part of the holiday season in New York City. Every year, the large tree st.
articles.body: For millions of people, the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree is a familiar part of the holiday season in New York City. Every year, the large tree stands in the plaza, decorated with lights and ornaments, before being taken down after the holidays. But its journey does not end there.Since 2007, lumber from the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree has been donated to Habitat for Humanity for use in housing projects. According to the organisation, the tree is milled into construction material and used to help build or improve Habitat homes.The programme is part of a longstanding partnership between Habitat for Humanity and Tishman Speyer, the owner and operator of Rockefeller Center. Tishman Speyer donates the tree's lumber to Habitat, while company staff members work alongside Habitat families on construction projects.The arrangement has connected a Christmas tradition seen by millions with homes where families can continue creating their own memories. Some homeowners have lumber from Rockefeller Center trees built directly into parts of their homes, making the history of the tree a permanent part of their houses.Rockefeller Center Christmas trees get a second lifeRockefeller Center usually selects a Norway Spruce for its annual Christmas display. After the holiday season, the trunk is milled into two-by-four and two-by-six beams. Tishman Speyer then donates the lumber.The wood is particularly useful for several parts of construction. Norway Spruce is more flexible and durable than lumber used for load-bearing walls. This makes it suitable for blocking, which means filling, spacing, joining or reinforcing parts of a frame.The lumber can also be used for flooring, furniture and cabinetry. Over the years, wood from Rockefeller Center Christmas trees has been used in homes in several communities, including locations in New York, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Mississippi and Maryland.Jonathan Reckford, CEO of the organisation, said the partnership gives the Christmas tree a purpose beyond the holiday season.“Tishman Speyer generously donates one of the largest and most widely-recognized Christmas trees to Habitat,” Reckford says. “The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree is a reminder to reflect, be thankful and to remember to give back to others among the hustle and bustle of the holidays. That symbol will live on as part of Habitat homeowners’ lives in their new houses.”The connection is also visible at Habitat's headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia. Several walls there feature exposed lumber from the 2018 Rockefeller Center Christmas tree. The wood carries stamps from different years commemorating the annual tree lighting ceremony.The first year of the programme was 2007. That year's Rockefeller Center tree came from Shelton, Connecticut, and its lumber was used in Habitat homes in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The programme continued through the following years.A Christmas tree becomes part of a family homeThe 2022 tree became part of Sarah'shome in Corinth, New York. Sarah and the Habitat volunteers used its lumber to build a detached side deck and two planter boxes.Sarah planned to use the deck as a place for her family to grill and spend time together. The planter boxes were used to grow vegetables, with Sarah and her daughters planting sweet pepper and carrot seeds.The wood also became a reminder of Sarah's long path towards homeownership. She said she had spent almost eight years improving her credit and savings before being able to purchase a home.“I worked on getting my credit up and improving my savings for almost eight years to be able to purchase a home,” Sarah says. “My kids can see that if you put effort into something, something will come out of it. I hope my kids gain patience and understanding that things don’t happen right away, that it does take time.”Another homeowner, Lakisha, has lumber from the 2017 Rockefeller Center tree in her New York home. Several exposed pieces in her pantry and cabinets carry a commemorative stamp marking the anniversary of Rockefeller Center's 85th tree lighting.“Every day, it’s a beautiful reminder of how far I’ve come,” Lakisha says. “And that you should never give up on your dreams, no matter what.”The 2025 Rockefeller Center tree came from East Greenbush, New York. Habitat said its lumber will be used in homes in communities to be announced in 2026.The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree tradition itself dates back to 1931, when workers excavating the site put up a 20-foot balsam fir. articles.summary: US News: A self-made billionaire couple gave San Francisco State University a $25 million gift, with a large portion of the donation made in XRP, making it one.
articles.body: A self-made billionaire couple gave San Francisco State University a $25 million gift, with a large portion of the donation made in XRP, making it one of the biggest cryptocurrency contributions to US higher education at the time. Chris Larsen, an SF State alumnus, and his wife Lyna Lam donated to the Rippleworks Foundation in April 2019. The gift established funds for the university’s College of Business and supported new initiatives focused on innovation, entrepreneurship and financial technology. According to San Francisco State University, the XRP contribution was the institution’s first digital asset donation and ranked among the largest digital asset gifts made to a US university. The donation also led California State University to rename the College of Business the Lam Family College of Business. The couple had supported SF State since 2001, with previous contributions exceeding $800,000 for scholarships, education, science and business initiatives.How did San Francisco State get its first $25 million XRP donationIn April 2019, San Francisco State University President Leslie E. Wong announced the $25 million donation from Chris Larsen, Lyna Lam and the Rippleworks Foundation. The gift established the Chris Larsen and Lyna Lam Funds for the College of Business, intended to strengthen the college’s ability to respond to changes in the business sector. The university said the contribution would also help prepare students for careers as business innovators and entrepreneurs.A large portion of the donation was made in XRP, which the university described as the first digital asset donation in SF State’s history. The gift was also among the largest donations made in digital assets to a US university at the time. The use of XRP distinguished the contribution from conventional university donations made through cash, securities or other traditional assets. At the same time, the funds were directed towards the university’s business education and innovation programmes.The $25 million gift led to a college renamingThe contribution also resulted in the renaming of San Francisco State University’s College of Business. California State University announced that the college would become the Lam Family College of Business in recognition of the Lam-Larsens’ long-term support and generosity. Chris Larsen, who graduated from SF State with a Bachelor of Science degree in 1984, and Lyna Lam had supported the university since 2001.The $25 million contribution was part of the couple's broader record of giving. Larsen and Lam had donated more than $800,000 to scholarships, education, science and business initiatives across the university, in addition to their gifts to the College of Business. Their previous support included the Chris Larsen Scholarship Fund in the Graduate College of Education and funding for initiatives in the Biology Department within the College of Science and Engineering.Donation launched five new business initiativesPart of the donation established the Lam-Larsen Fund for Global Innovation. The fund was created to bring students, faculty, alumni and outside experts together across disciplines to exchange ideas, explore entrepreneurship and work on solutions to practical problems. The university said the programme was intended to encourage global awareness while helping students develop an understanding of innovation and responsible business leadership.The fund supported five new initiatives within the College of Business: the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Initiative, Emerging and Developing Economies Initiative, Financial Technology Initiative, Business and Education Technology Initiative, and Centre for Workforce of the Future. These initiatives were designed to expand opportunities for students and faculty to work across areas including entrepreneurship, financial technology, education technology and workforce development.Gift honoured Lyna Lam’s family historyThe university’s account of the donation also links the Lam-Larsen family’s support to Lyna Lam’s family history. The Lam family, including Lyna’s father Quang Lam, left Cambodia after he led his family’s escape from war and genocide. The family spent time in refugee camps in Thailand and the Philippines before immigrating to the United States and settling in the Bay Area. The university said the Lam Family College of Business was named in honour of Lyna’s family at Chris Larsen’s recommendation.The $25 million donation was also a lead gift for SF State’s BOLD Thinking campaign. The campaign was more than 90 per cent funded when the donation was announced. The university said the contribution was intended to support its efforts in business innovation and entrepreneurship, while building on the Lam-Larsens’ previous financial support for scholarships and academic programmes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1963, Rat Pack composer Jimmy Van Heusen bought a secluded California mountain; decades later it became a legendary celebrity hideaway
articles.summary: US News: Some places become famous because of what they look like, and then there are places whose reputation comes almost entirely from the people who once ga.
articles.body: Some places become famous because of what they look like, and then there are places whose reputation comes almost entirely from the people who once gathered there. High above Yucca Valley in California’s high desert, Rattlesnake Ranch belongs firmly to the second category. Composer Jimmy Van Heusen bought the secluded mountaintop in 1963, seeking the privacy that increasingly eluded Hollywood stars in nearby Palm Springs. What followed was a remarkable chapter in Rat Pack history, as the retreat became associated with Van Heusen’s close friends Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby, as well as visits from President John F. Kennedy. Today, after years of decline, the once-secret hideaway is being restored as a luxury rental, giving a new generation a glimpse into one of Hollywood’s most colourful desert escapes.Why Jimmy Van Heusen escaped Hollywood for Yucca ValleyVan Heusen was far more than a composer living in the shadow of the stars he wrote for. A four-time Oscar winner, he created enduring songs including Come Fly with Me, Call Me Irresponsible and All the Way. According to the data on the official site, his professional and personal friendship with Frank Sinatra placed him firmly inside the world that would become synonymous with the Rat Pack. By the early 1960s, however, Palm Springs no longer offered the isolation that celebrities wanted. The desert resort had become so popular with Hollywood figures and tourists that privacy was increasingly difficult to find. Van Heusen went further into the high desert and chose a mountain overlooking Yucca Valley. The finished retreat became known variously as Scenic Mountain, JVH Ranch and, eventually, Rattlesnake Ranch. The setting was almost perfectly suited to the lifestyle Van Heusen had cultivated, isolated, difficult to stumble upon, and far removed from Hollywood's watchful eyes.The secluded mountain became a Rat Pack escapeRattlesnake Ranch soon developed a reputation considerably larger than its remote location. Sinatra was among Van Heusen's closest friends and collaborators, and the mountain became one of the places where members of the Hollywood set could disappear from public view. SFGATE visited the property during its restoration and describes the ranch as a place where Sinatra, Crosby and Kennedy were among the famous guests. The atmosphere was tied closely to the excesses associated with the Rat Pack era, with Van Heusen embracing a famously hard-living bachelor lifestyle. The ranch's isolation was part of its attraction. Unlike Palm Springs, no neighbouring homes were crowding the mountain. Guests could arrive, stay and party away from the photographers and Hollywood insiders who surrounded celebrities elsewhere. Van Heusen's connection to Sinatra was particularly important. His songs helped define the singer's catalogue, while Sinatra's former valet George Jacobs later portrayed Van Heusen as an influential figure in the singer's lifestyle as well as his professional circle. The composer became such a character in Yucca Valley that locals embraced him, and he was named honorary mayor in 1967, with actor Henry Fonda reportedly attending the ceremony.The JFK and Marilyn Monroe story has a catchPerhaps the most enduring legend attached to Rattlesnake Ranch involves John F. Kennedy and Marilyn Monroe. The story has long suggested that the president and Monroe had an encounter at the secluded property. Both had genuine connections to Van Heusen. His song High Hopes became Kennedy's 1960 campaign song, while Van Heusen composed music for Monroe's film Let's Make Love. Kennedy also definitely visited Van Heusen's Yucca Valley home, according to contemporary reports. But one crucial detail makes the famous story difficult to accept, Monroe died in 1962, while the house was not completed until 1963. The better-documented links between Kennedy and Monroe point elsewhere in the Palm Springs area. That has not stopped the legend from becoming part of the ranch's identity. The restored pool house now includes a bedroom inspired by Monroe, while another room pays tribute to Sinatra. The property effectively preserves both the history and mythology surrounding its most famous visitors.Van Heusen eventually left, and the ranch fell into disrepairThe party years did not last forever. Van Heusen married Bobbe Brock in 1969, and the composer subsequently described a much quieter married life. He eventually sold his mountaintop retreat and returned to the Palm Springs area. The property later operated as the Scenic Mountain Club, including a restaurant, before eventually closing. For years, Rattlesnake Ranch sat largely abandoned. Thomas Cribb bought the property in 2006. By then, the main house was already in an uninhabitable condition, but the extraordinary views and complete privacy of the mountain convinced him that the place could have another life. Even in its rougher state, the property retained its pull. The pool house had been rented to visitors, and according to Cribb, it was booked more than 300 nights a year despite its rustic condition.Rattlesnake Ranch is being reborn as a luxury desert retreatThe latest chapter is transforming the old celebrity hideaway into a carefully restored luxury property. The renovated pool house contains two bedrooms and two bathrooms and sleeps up to six people. Its design combines contemporary comforts with mid-century influences and archival photographs from Van Heusen's era. The original pool and barbecue pit have been retained, while the grounds now include a stone hot tub, sunken fire pit and a two-person swing overlooking Yucca Valley. The restoration is also deliberately preserving details that connect visitors to the ranch's past. According to the developers, the pool where Sinatra and Kennedy reportedly swam remains in place, allowing the property to retain physical links to its celebrity history. The main house is planned for a larger restoration, with four bedrooms and the return of Van Heusen's distinctive pink hot tub in the living room.Once completed, the entire mountain is expected to operate as a single rental for private stays, weddings and events. There is also a striking reminder of just how seriously Kennedy's security was taken. The property has two helicopter landing areas, with the second reportedly added after the Secret Service considered the original landing arrangement unsuitable. The main house also contained an extraordinary 37 telephone lines for the presidential visits. What remains at Rattlesnake Ranch, then, is more than an old Hollywood house. It is a physical reminder of an era when composers, singers, actors and political leaders could retreat into the desert and temporarily create a private world of their own. As the ranch moves from abandoned hideaway to restored luxury retreat, its greatest selling point remains unchanged from 1963, an entire mountain, far from everyone else.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Daniel Craig beyond James Bond: How the Hollywood actor became a global advocate against landmines
articles.summary: When someone mentions Daniel Craig, most people still picture a dashing man in a black tux, cool as ice as he dodges supervillains and explosions, wit.
articles.body: When someone mentions Daniel Craig, most people still picture a dashing man in a black tux, cool as ice as he dodges supervillains and explosions, with an almost supernatural ability to escape danger. Offscreen, though, he took on something more sobering and a lot riskier in real life when he stepped up as the UN’s first Global Advocate for the Elimination of Mines and Explosive Hazards.For the unversed, Craig’s formal role started in 2015, when then-UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon appointed him the organisation’s first UN Global Advocate for the Elimination of Mines and Explosive Hazards. Eight years later, when his stint ended in 2023, Craig had helped raise over $1 million and turned what could have been a forgettable PR gig into something that really mattered.Daniel Craig's UN role: From James Bond to mine-action advocateIn April 2015, the United Nations gave Craig a very different kind of mission from anything he had played on screen. Craig’s real job wasn’t just to talk about the dangers of mines on some world stage. He actually traveled to affected countries, walked through minefields in places like Cyprus, and watched as deminers put their lives on the line, exploding ordnance left buried under the soil.According to the UN, Craig participated in international meetings, visited mine-clearance operations, produced public-awareness messages and helped mobilise resources for the UN Trust Fund for Assistance in Mine Action. The UN says he helped raise more than $1 million for mine action during his tenure.It’s almost a full circle when you think about it: the guy trained to act cool around stunt explosions is suddenly surrounded by landmines that don’t give second takes.Why do landmines remain dangerous?Now, as for landmines, they mess with lives for decades after the shooting stops. They can trap communities, keep farmers away from fields, and force kids to tiptoe to school. The worst part? According to the UN's mine-action programme, these weapons are a threat not only to individual lives but also to economic recovery. These hazards slow down entire economies and keep displaced families from ever going home again. Clearing them isn’t just heroic; sometimes it’s the only thing that lets a place heal.That is why humanitarian mine action involves much more than finding and destroying explosives. It includes surveying contaminated land, marking dangerous areas, clearing mines, educating communities about risks, and supporting survivors.That’s why Craig’s gigs went well beyond public service announcements.Daniel Craig went into the minefields himselfWhile doing his part, Craig put a face to the Unexploded Ordnance problem and the UN’s Safe Ground campaign, which aims to turn contaminated land back into playgrounds and farms. It wasn’t exactly a Bond movie, but there was real danger and real hope there.And the scale of the problem was massive. Countries from Afghanistan to Colombia, across Africa and the Middle East, were riddled with explosives that wouldn’t quit. That’s why advocacy by someone as visible as Craig matters because landmines aren’t news-friendly unless someone famous drags the world’s attention back to them.The real-world stakes behind the campaignWhat Craig did best was clarify: these ugly leftovers don’t “end” when peace breaks out. A landmine can kill decades later, long after the generals sign the treaties and the headlines move on. Craig used his spotlight to make sure people who work every day to clear these hazards are recognized, supported, and, if he has his way, never forgotten.He wrapped up his time as the UN’s top anti-landmine advocate in April 2023, reminding the world that an invisible danger is sometimes the deadliest. Unlike a Bond villain, a landmine will wait forever for its victim. Thanks to Craig, that’s a little harder for everyone to ignore.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Dakota Johnson's home is a vintage, jungly abode cradled with colourful plant friends: 10 beautiful indoor plants that fill her home
articles.summary: Dakota Johnson is a popular Hollywood actress, best known for her work in the 50 Shades of Grey trilogy. Her Los Angeles home isn't your typical Holly.
articles.body: Dakota Johnson is a popular Hollywood actress, best known for her work in the 50 Shades of Grey trilogy. Her Los Angeles home isn't your typical Hollywood mansion. It's a mid-century retreat, once designed by architect Carl Maston, that Johnson herself calls her "anchor".She gave a glimpse into her house in a home tour series by Architectural Digest some time ago, and her home is nothing less than a vintage retreat.Her place gives a clean vibe and is a cosy retreat, filled with vintage furniture, personal mementos, and lined with numerous plants and flowering pots that give a lively energy to her space, tucked carefully into nearly every corner.Here are some indoor plants that line Dakota Johnson’s jungly-vintage abodeThe delicate fernsThe maidenhair fern is a delicate houseplant with thin black stems and fan-shaped, nearly feathery leaves that flutter with the slightest breeze.This face-shaped pot is kept in her kitchen where she cooks and bakes most of the time.The button fern is a sturdier, more forgiving cousin, with small, round, glossy leaflets that look almost like a string of coins along each frond. It grows in lower light better than most ferns and doesn't demand constant attention, making it ideal for shelves or low tables. This one is placed right next to its cousin on the kitchen slab in her home.Long and short green friendsThe burgundy rubber tree brings deep, wine-coloured leaves and an upright silhouette that can single-handedly anchor a living room or reading nook. It grows best in bright, indirect light and only needs watering once the top layer of soil dries out, making it fairly low-maintenance for how dramatic it looks. This plant adds character to Johnson’s living room, placed right next to her sofa and center table.Mimosa, a tiny yellow plant with fern-like leaves that fold shut when touched, brings a playful element. A potful of these is placed right next to her living room doorway, enjoys bright light and regular watering, and is often grown outdoors. A potted mimosa near a sunny window can be a fun conversation starter indoors, especially in homes with kids or curious guests.Romantic bloomsPeonies are the epitome of romantic, old-world charm, with their full, ruffled petals and heady fragrance. They're technically a seasonal cut flower rather than a houseplant. A vase of peonies lines the entrance next to her dog’s portrait on a console table that instantly elevates a space, echoing the same warm, collected feel of her vintage home.The Persian buttercup lines the same pot at the entrance, with layered, paper-thin petals in shades of red, pink, orange, and white, offering a similar softness with a slightly wilder edge.The bohemian bundleThe butterfly ranunculus looks almost like a rose crossed with tissue paper, with delicate, crinkled petals that catch the light beautifully and are rightly placed at her table in the wood-paneled office. It's a slightly rarer variety than the standard ranunculus, making it a lovely choice for a smaller, more intentional arrangement.Anemones line the same pot on Johnson’s table, with their dark centres and crisp, poppy-like petals, which bring a graphic, slightly wild quality to any flower arrangement.The bedroom brightsGoldenrods, with their feathery yellow plumes, are an easy way to bring warmth and texture into a room, especially in the cooler months. They're often used as a filler flower in bouquets, but a handful of these line a table in Dakota’s bedroom.Along with the gerbera daisies, which are the easiest way to bring instant colour into a home. With their bold, rounded petals in shades of orange, red and yellow.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: A 12-foot Burmese python revealed Florida’s bizarre new method for finding hidden invasive snakes after it swallowed a collared opossum
articles.summary: US News: Deep in the forests of Florida’s Key Largo, an opossum is being used to find an animal that researchers rarely see coming. Fitted with a small trackin.
articles.body: Deep in the forests of Florida’s Key Largo, an opossum is being used to find an animal that researchers rarely see coming. Fitted with a small tracking collar and released back into the wild, the marsupial goes about its normal movements through the undergrowth. The collar is programmed to notice when that movement suddenly stops. If the signal later starts travelling again, it can point scientists towards a Burmese python carrying the device inside its body. The unusual method grew out of a mammal-tracking project rather than a plan to hunt snakes.A strange signal in 2022 led researchers to a large female python that had swallowed a collared opossum, revealing that the transmitter could continue working inside the snake. Since then, the approach has been developed into a practical way of locating some of Florida’s largest invasive pythons, which can be exceptionally difficult to spot in the Everglades.Florida researchers discover a strange new way to track hidden pythonsAs reported by South Florida Sun Sentinel, the idea did not begin as a python-hunting technique. In 2022, Michael Cove, curator of mammals at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences, was studying how raccoons and opossums used Crocodile Lake National Wildlife Refuge. Then one of the collars behaved strangely.A mortality signal indicated that an animal had stopped moving. That might have meant a road accident, an attack by another animal or some other cause of death. But the signal later began travelling again. It stopped, moved, stopped again.That pattern was difficult to explain if the collar was still attached to the opossum. It made much more sense if the animal had been eaten and the collar had remained inside its predator. The likely culprit was a Burmese python.Tracking the signal was not straightforward. Key Largo is built on ancient coral rock, with a landscape containing holes, cavities and places where a large snake can remain concealed. It took about a month before the team located the animal responsible.They eventually recovered a female python measuring about 12 feet long and weighing roughly 66 pounds. It had egg follicles, indicating that it was a reproductive female. The collar was still intact inside the snake and transmitting a signal.How a swallowed collar keeps tracking Florida pythons from insideBurmese pythons have a useful weakness from the perspective of the tracking system: they digest large meals slowly.A collar swallowed with an opossum does not immediately disappear. Instead, it remains inside the python while the snake digests its meal. That gives researchers time to follow the signal.The important sequence is the change in behaviour. A collar first reports that its animal has stopped moving. Later, the signal itself starts appearing in different locations. For biologists, that combination can indicate that the opossum has been eaten and that the predator carrying the collar has moved.The team began developing the accidental discovery into a more deliberate method. Grant support from the South Florida Water Management District helped turn the experiment into a larger field operation, while Southern Illinois University graduate researcher A.J. Sanjar became involved in working out how the technique could be used more effectively.According to the Washington Times, the equipment also became cheaper. Early collars could cost around $1,500. Later versions were available for about $190, making it much easier to consider fitting larger numbers of animals.Why Florida researchers release collared opossums where pythons are huntingThe opossums are deliberately fitted with collars because they are potential prey for Burmese pythons. After being captured, however, they are returned to the same habitat rather than moved somewhere unfamiliar.That distinction matters to the researchers because the animals would still be exposed to predators, vehicles and other hazards in the wild. The collar allows the team to learn what happens when one disappears.According to CBS12 News, Jeremy Dixon, manager of the wildlife refuge, has defended the approach by pointing out that the danger faced by the opossums already exists. The research is intended to reveal when one has been taken by a python and use that event to locate the snake.Still, the method raises an obvious question: does fitting an animal with tracking equipment and releasing it as a potential meal amount to deliberately putting it in danger? There is no simple way around that question. The project depends on a predator eating the very animal carrying the device.How collared opossums lead Florida researchers to large Burmese pythonsThe choice of opossums has another advantage. A large Burmese python can swallow a surprisingly substantial meal, while a smaller snake cannot. A collared opossum therefore works, in effect, as a size filter. The system is more likely to lead researchers towards a python capable of consuming it.That is useful because large females are particularly important targets. Burmese pythons can produce large numbers of eggs, so removing a mature female can prevent a substantial number of young snakes from entering the population.By April 2026, the project had been credited with helping locate and remove 18 Burmese pythons. Every one was more than eight feet long, with the largest measuring around 13 feet.Dixon said, “These are all reproductively viable pythons.”At that stage, 32 opossums had been fitted with collars, with the team aiming to increase that number to at least 40 during the summer.One python apparently provided an especially clear demonstration of how the system could work. A 12-foot snake was found to have swallowed two collared opossums, producing two separate mortality signals from essentially the same location.Florida has tried dogs, drones and scout snakes to find hidden pythonsThe opossum system sits within a much larger effort to locate Burmese pythons, which have become firmly established across southern Florida.Finding them is difficult because the snakes are well camouflaged and can remain out of sight for long periods. Researchers and wildlife managers have consequently tried several different approaches, including detector dogs, drones, thermal imaging and specially trained male pythons that can act as scouts. There have even been attempts involving robotic prey.The difficulty is partly a matter of scale. The Everglades contains vast stretches of wetland, forest and difficult terrain, much of it unsuitable for people searching on foot. A python does not need to move far or make much noise to avoid being detected.That makes an animal which naturally travels through the same habitat an intriguing tracking device.Florida’s unusual python tracker does not always lead to a snakeThe method is far from foolproof. In one case, a collar produced the expected mortality signal before beginning to move again. Researchers followed it, expecting to find a python. Instead, they encountered fresh snake faeces and the collar.The python had apparently swallowed the opossum, retained the collar long enough for it to transmit and then passed the device. By the time researchers arrived, the snake had gone.There have also been collars that simply disappeared. At one stage, three of 43 deployed collars were confirmed to have been eaten, while six could no longer be located. So the signal does not always end with a captured python. Sometimes it becomes a trail that goes cold.How Florida researchers adapted their collars to track hidden pythonsThe equipment has also changed as the researchers learned what information they actually needed.The early approach relied on GPS movement data. But once the basic trick was understood, detailed movement histories were less important. The key requirement was knowing where the collar was when researchers needed to find it.By 2026, the project had moved towards simpler VHF transmitters rather than full GPS tracking. Their batteries could last close to two years, reducing the amount of maintenance required in the field.The collar does not need to tell researchers everywhere a snake has travelled. It only needs to remain inside the snake long enough to point towards it.Why Florida’s Burmese pythons are a growing concern for native wildlifeThe research published in PNAS, titled ‘Severe mammal declines coincide with proliferation of invasive Burmese pythons in Everglades National Park’ revealed that Burmese pythons have had particularly severe effects on native mammals in the Everglades. A long-running road survey published in 2012 recorded dramatic declines in sightings of several species inside Everglades National Park, including raccoons, opossums and bobcats. Opossum observations fell by 98.9% in the survey, while raccoon sightings declined by 99.3%.Those figures should not be read as a statewide population census. They came from a specific road survey within the national park. Even so, the scale of the recorded change illustrates the ecological pressure associated with the spread of the snakes.The US Geological Survey has also documented substantial impacts from invasive pythons on native wildlife in south Florida.Against that background, the collared-opossum experiment is less about finding a clever gadget and more about solving a basic problem: how do you locate an animal that is exceptionally good at remaining unseen?For the researchers, the answer has turned out to involve another animal moving through the same landscape. An opossum walks into the forest with a transmitter around its neck. Somewhere out there, a python may be watching.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: San Diego high school students created 39 wildlife gardens in just 4 years; now nearly 25,000 sq ft of habitat supports native plants and pollinators
articles.summary: US News: Nearly 350 San Diego high-school students have spent the past four years turning school grounds and community spaces into native wildlife gardens, hel.
articles.body: Nearly 350 San Diego high-school students have spent the past four years turning school grounds and community spaces into native wildlife gardens, helping create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens. The work is part of the Native Biodiversity Corps, a San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance programme launched in 2022 to give students hands-on experience in conservation. Participants learn about native plants, wildlife and habitat restoration before designing, planting and maintaining gardens with guidance from conservation professionals. The gardens are intended to provide resources for pollinators and other local wildlife in urban areas while giving students practical conservation skills. The programme has also expanded beyond schools, with students helping transform an unused golf-course space into a native garden.How San Diego students created 39 wildlife gardensThe Native Biodiversity Corps began in spring 2022 with funding from San Diego's Level Up programme. More than 300 urban high-school students registered within 72 hours, while about 100 students were selected for the inaugural programme. Participants spent the summer visiting conservation sites including the San Diego Zoo, San Diego Zoo Safari Park, San Diego Natural History Museum, Living Coast Discovery Center and San Elijo Lagoon Ecological Reserve. They then used what they had learned to design and build native wildlife gardens at Crawford, Hoover and Lincoln high schools.Students are involved in more than simply planting vegetation. They survey potential garden locations, develop designs, select suitable native plants, help implement the projects and participate in maintaining the gardens. The programme gives them an opportunity to learn about local ecosystems while working alongside conservation professionals and applying ecological concepts in real-world settings.Nearly 25,000 sq ft of habitat restoredAccording to San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance's September 2026 update, nearly 350 students have participated in the Native Biodiversity Corps since its launch. Together, they have helped create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens on school grounds and elsewhere across San Diego County.The figure represents the combined area of multiple gardens rather than one continuous wildlife reserve. The projects vary in size and location, but they share an emphasis on using native vegetation to create habitat and ecological resources within developed areas.Native plants support pollinatorsA central aim of the gardens is to provide food and habitat for pollinators and other wildlife. At Hoover High School, students transformed a tree planter into a pollinator garden containing California poppy, narrowleaf milkweed, showy penstemon and California buckwheat.The use of native plants is important because they are adapted to the region's environmental conditions and can provide resources for species that have evolved alongside them. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says the gardens can also contribute to habitat corridors, creating a network of smaller green spaces that can provide resources for wildlife moving through urban areas.Students transformed unused spacesSome of the projects have involved spaces that previously provided little habitat. At Crawford High School, students transformed an undeveloped hillside into a green space. At another location, students created a native garden on a previously bare hillside, with the goal of providing habitat resources for local pollinators.The projects give students direct responsibility for changing their surroundings. Instead of learning about biodiversity solely through textbooks, they can observe how plants develop and how wildlife responds as the gardens mature.The project expanded beyond school campusesThe students' conservation work has increasingly moved into wider community spaces. In one project, Native Biodiversity Corps participants worked with Pro Kids, First Tee to transform an unused chipping range at Colina Park Golf Course into a waterwise native garden containing 27 different native plant species.During the 2026 summer programme, students also worked with the San Diego Zoo Safari Park's horticulture team to design and install a native wildlife garden at the Beckman Center for Conservation Research. These projects have allowed students to take the skills learned at school and apply them to larger community and conservation settings.San Diego schools increased native plant optionsThe programme has also contributed to changes in school landscaping. When the initiative began, San Diego Unified School District had four native plant species approved for use on its campuses, according to the Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Through collaboration involving students, teachers, administrators and conservation specialists, that number has grown to nearly 30 native plant species.The development means the programme's influence has extended beyond individual gardens. Students have been involved in a broader effort to increase the use of native vegetation across school environments.The programme has grown since 2022The latest figures show how quickly the initiative has expanded. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance's 2024 annual report recorded 60 Native Biodiversity Corps students from three partner high schools, who designed and planted native gardens and helped create or restore more than 8,600 square feet of native wildlife habitat through 18 gardens.Its 2025 annual report subsequently recorded 180 students creating 10 native gardens during that reporting period. Students also participated in other conservation activities, including distributing native seedlings, supporting butterfly conservation and planting 10 trees with San Diego's Urban Forestry team.The latest September 2026 update puts the cumulative programme totals at nearly 350 students, 39 gardens and almost 25,000 square feet of created or restored habitat.Students are learning about conservation careersThe programme is designed to provide students with more than gardening experience. Participants work with conservation scientists, horticulturists and other specialists, giving them exposure to careers involving wildlife, plants, habitat restoration and environmental education.One participant, Gabi, joined the programme during its inaugural year and continued through 2026 before going to college to study landscape architecture. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says other students have also developed an interest in conservation and environmental careers as a result of their experience.The programme also provides financial recognition for students' work. According to the Zoo Wildlife Alliance, students who successfully complete a session and maintain active participation can be eligible for stipends of up to $2,000.This allows students to gain practical conservation experience while receiving support for the time they commit to the programme.San Diego County is recognised for its exceptional biodiversity, but urban development has fragmented many natural habitats. Native gardens cannot replace large protected ecosystems, but they can provide smaller patches of vegetation and resources within developed landscapes. The Native Biodiversity Corps uses school campuses and community spaces to create these pockets of native habitat. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says the network of gardens can help provide resources for pollinators and other wildlife and potentially contribute to habitat connectivity across urban areas.A four-year effort that continues to growWhat began in 2022 as a conservation programme for high-school students has developed into a county-wide initiative involving nearly 350 young people. In four years, participants have helped create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens, while gaining practical experience in native planting, habitat restoration and biodiversity conservation.The programme's impact therefore extends beyond the gardens themselves. Students leave behind native plantings that can be maintained by future cohorts while carrying conservation knowledge into their further education and careers. The result is a growing network of small habitat patches created by students who began the programme by learning about biodiversity and ended up helping put those lessons into practice.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A $25 million Boca Raton mansion now has AI running the home; inside the futuristic Florida property with 150 feet of waterfront
articles.summary: News News: Artificial intelligence is moving beyond phones, computers and workplaces and into some of the world's most expensive homes. A newly listed mansion in.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is moving beyond phones, computers and workplaces and into some of the world's most expensive homes. A newly listed mansion in Boca Raton, Florida, offers a striking example of that shift, combining luxury waterfront living with an extensive smart-home system designed to control much of the property. According to realtor.com, the two-story residence, listed for $24.995 million, has six bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms and approximately 10,814 square feet of interior living space. The home uses Josh AI alongside Lutron, Sonos and Crestron technology to control features including lighting, window shades, sound and climate. The property also has six remotely accessible security cameras and sits along 150 feet of Intracoastal Waterway frontage.A waterfront home built around technologyLocated at 2401 Spanish River Road, the Boca Raton estate sits on nearly half an acre and underwent a major transformation in 2024. The redesign turned the property into a contemporary waterfront retreat, combining modern architecture with technology intended to make everyday life easier. The home's artificial intelligence system is one of its most unusual features. Rather than relying only on conventional switches and controls, the system allows residents to interact with the home using voice commands. Josh AI works alongside other smart-home technologies to manage different parts of the property.Lighting, window shades, audio and climate controls can all be integrated into the system. Security is also connected, with six cameras that can be monitored remotely. The idea is to allow the technology to operate quietly in the background while residents control the home's environment with minimal effort. But despite its high-tech systems, the property is designed to feel more like a luxury resort than a futuristic laboratory.Inside the $25 million mansionThe home's 2024 redesign was overseen by Umber Architecture, with interiors by Eric Dyer of Arthur Collection and construction by BNK Construction. The design combines pale stone, warm wood and large areas of glass, creating interiors that emphasise the waterfront setting. Ten-foot ceilings run through the main floor, while marmorino plaster adds texture to the walls. A custom staircase with stone treads serves as an architectural focal point as visitors move through the main entertaining areas.According to realtor.com, the home features a spacious 44-by-29-foot great room and a separate living room that extends more than 32 feet in length. The dining room covers roughly 21 by 20 feet, providing substantial space for entertaining. The kitchen, approximately 30 feet long, is another major feature. It is centred around Brazilian Casablanca quartzite and includes integrated Miele and Sub-Zero appliances. Custom cabinetry allows parts of the kitchen to be concealed when not in use, helping maintain the clean appearance of the room. There is also a second kitchen for preparation, along with a wine room capable of holding 214 bottles. An elevator, wet bar, custom closets and an air-conditioned three-car garage add to the home's amenities.A resort-style private retreatUpstairs, the primary suite continues the home's hotel-inspired design. The bedroom features custom woodwork, a sitting area and a balcony overlooking the Intracoastal Waterway. Its bathroom uses Belvedere quartzite and includes a steam shower, soaking tub, vanity and a large dressing area. Five additional bedrooms are spread throughout the house, including one on the main level.Outside, the property is designed for entertaining as much as relaxing. The backyard features a heated saltwater swimming pool, covered loggia, pergola, summer kitchen and built-in barbecue. Multiple patios, terraces, balconies and a deck provide different areas for enjoying the gardens and waterfront views. The landscaping includes California olive trees, while the property also has a private dock and ocean access. Both the seawall and dock were completed in 2024. Additional systems include a generator, tankless water heater and water purification system.With its combination of waterfront access, resort-style interiors and AI-assisted home controls, the Boca Raton property reflects how technology is becoming part of the luxury-home experience. For a buyer willing to spend nearly $25 million, the appeal is not simply having a smart home, but having a residence where many everyday functions can be managed through an integrated system, while the architecture and waterfront setting remain central to the property's appeal.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Meet Cameron Myers, the 20-year-old Australian who beat two Olympic champions to win the Diamond League 1,500m final in 3:30.14
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At just 20, Australian middle-distance runner Cameron Myers has produced the biggest victory of his young career, winning the men's 1,500 metres at th.
articles.body: At just 20, Australian middle-distance runner Cameron Myers has produced the biggest victory of his young career, winning the men's 1,500 metres at the 2026 Diamond League Final in Brussels. Myers clocked 3:30.14, edging Kenya's Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech by just 0.04 seconds in a dramatic finish. According to Reuters and Adelaide Now, Myers overcame a field packed with some of the world's leading middle-distance runners, including the two most recent Olympic champions in the event, American Cole Hocker and Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen. Hocker finished seventh in 3:30.80, while Ingebrigtsen placed fourth in 3:30.52. The victory made Myers only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League Final and capped a breakthrough season in which he has established himself as one of the country's most promising middle-distance athletes.A dramatic finish in BrusselsThe men's 1,500m final brought together a remarkably strong field, with Olympic champions, international medal contenders and several of the world's fastest runners lining up in Brussels. Myers entered the race as one of Australia's rising stars, but the quality of the field presented an enormous challenge. The race remained tightly contested through the final stages. Myers positioned himself within striking distance before making his decisive move in the home straight. That strategy paid off. Myers produced a powerful finishing kick to overtake the runners around him and narrowly beat Koech to the line. Myers finished in 3:30.14, Koech in 3:30.18 and American Ethan Strand in 3:30.50. Ingebrigtsen followed in fourth with 3:30.52, while Yared Nuguse, Hobbs Kessler and Hocker completed the next three places. The margin between first and second was only four hundredths of a second, highlighting just how close the race became in its final metres.Myers' rapid riseThe Brussels victory did not come out of nowhere. Myers has been building an impressive résumé throughout 2026 and has steadily established himself among the world's elite 1,500m runners. One defining moment of his season came in June at the Paris Diamond League meeting, where he ran 3:28.00 to set an Australian national record. That performance also ranked among the fastest 1,500m times in the world this year. He later won the mile at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene, recording 3:46.06.Myers also earned a silver medal in the mile at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, finishing behind Scottish world-record holder Josh Kerr. Just days before the Diamond League Final, he won the 1,500m at the ISTAF meeting in Berlin in 3:30.96. His consistency across different competitions has helped transform him from a promising young Australian runner into a serious international contender.Beating Olympic championsWhat made the Brussels victory particularly significant was the strength of the athletes Myers defeated. Ingebrigtsen won the Olympic 1,500m title at the Tokyo Games, while Hocker captured Olympic gold in the event at Paris 2024. Both were expected to be major contenders in Brussels, yet neither finished on the podium. Ingebrigtsen crossed the line fourth in 3:30.52, while Hocker finished seventh in 3:30.80. The result demonstrated that Myers could compete successfully against established champions rather than simply winning when the biggest names were absent. The Australian's victory also came in a race where the top seven runners all finished within less than a second of one another, making his ability to time his final acceleration particularly important.A new chapter for Australian athleticsMyers' Diamond League triumph represents another important milestone for Australian middle-distance running. The official Diamond League profile now lists him as a Diamond League Final winner and records his personal best of 3:28.00 in the 1,500m. The 20-year-old's rise has been especially notable due to his rapid progression. His national record in Paris, international victories and Commonwealth Games medals have all come in a single breakthrough season. His Brussels victory now adds one of the sport's most prestigious annual titles to that record. More importantly, beating two Olympic champions in a tightly fought final suggests Myers is no longer simply viewed as Australia's next big middle-distance prospect. He has already shown that he can deliver when competing against the best in the world, and at only 20, he may have several more years to build on that breakthrough.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Satya Niketan PG collapse: Congress slams BJP, calls 'four-engine government’ a ‘killing machine’
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Monday launched a scathing attack on the BJP government, alleging that corruption and administrative negligence led to the .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Monday launched a scathing attack on the BJP government, alleging that corruption and administrative negligence led to the collapse of a five-storey PG building near Delhi University’s South Campus on Sunday.Seven people have been killed in the tragedy so far, with the opposition demanding accountability and action against those responsible.Addressing a press conference, Congress leader and NSUI in-charge Kanhaiya Kumar demanded action against all those responsible for the collapse. The party also sought affordable accommodation for students, a rent control law for hostels and paying guest (PG) facilities, and compensation of Rs 1 crore for the families of those killed.“There is no information on how many people are still trapped under the debris. The PG had 45 beds. It was Sunday — what if all the students were there?” he said.‘Modi went to SRCC for PR, why not Satya Niketan?’Kumar accused the BJP-led government of prioritising publicity over accountability, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Delhi University’s Shri Ram College of Commerce (SRCC) on Saturday.“Prime Minister Modi has time to send congratulatory messages to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni but no time to visit Satya Niketan to express his condolences,” Kumar said, news agency PTI reported.Taking a swipe at the BJP’s description of governance through a “four-engine government”, Kumar said, “The four-engine government of the BJP is a killing machine — it is your MCD, your mayor, your MLA, you have a government in Delhi and an LG, you are the PM.”He alleged that the government had failed to take responsibility for a series of incidents in which students had lost their lives, including fires at coaching centres, flooding in libraries and electrocution incidents.“The question is — when will the BJP government take responsibility and accountability for this?” he asked.Congress alleges nexus over illegal PGsKumar also alleged that while BJP offices had been built to high standards, public infrastructure continued to deteriorate.“The BJP has constructed five-star party offices in every district which don’t collapse, but bridges fall, roads break and government buildings collapse,” he said.He alleged that corruption was behind the Satya Niketan collapse and claimed that the incident had exposed the gap between the government’s publicity campaigns and ground realities.“The PR balloon that PM Modi inflated a day before has been deflated by this act of God,” Kumar said.He said questions would have to be answered by Prime Minister Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah, Delhi CM Rekha Gupta, local MLAs, the mayor, councillors and the MCD commissioner.Kumar also questioned the role of Delhi University Vice Chancellor Yogesh Singh, alleging that he had frequently praised Modi.Police case, magisterial inquiry orderedThe NSUI has demanded that hostels be constructed within Delhi University, illegally operated hostels and PGs be shut down, and a rent control law be introduced for student accommodation.The five-storey building, which housed a boys’ paying guest accommodation, collapsed while repair work was underway. Police have registered a case against the building owner and others in connection with the incident.A magisterial inquiry has also been ordered to determine the circumstances leading to the collapse and fix responsibility.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
