articles.title: Ukraine turns to EU’s €90bn loan for US missiles as Patriot shield cracks under Russian barrage
articles.summary: International News: Ukraine has formally asked the European Union to use its €90 billion support loan to help fund the purchase of US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for .
articles.body: Ukraine has formally asked the European Union to use its €90 billion support loan to help fund the purchase of US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its Patriot air-defence systems, as Kyiv faces a critical shortage of interceptors amid continued Russian aerial attacks.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed the request in a post on X. “We will keep supporting Ukraine, including with European air defence and PAC-3 Patriot systems,” von der Leyen said.She added that the EU would “work closer than ever with Nato” to deter threats to European freedom and security.The request came as Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara pressed allies for additional military assistance. Khmara said Kyiv was also asking partner countries to allocate funds from their national budgets toward procuring Ukrainian-made drones.Ukraine currently faces a $27 billion defence budget shortfall, Khmara said, arguing that continued European support would ultimately benefit both Ukraine and its allies.“Every euro invested in Ukraine’s defence is an investment in European security,” he said.EU’s €90 billion Ukraine support loanThe European Council agreed in December 2025 to provide Ukraine with a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, aimed at covering the country’s urgent budgetary and defence needs. The Council finalised the legislation underpinning the loan on April 23, 2026, clearing the way for the European Commission to begin disbursing the funds.Under the framework, €30 billion is earmarked for macroeconomic support and can be used to meet Ukraine’s immediate budgetary requirements. The remaining €60 billion is intended to strengthen Ukraine’s defence-industrial capacity and finance the procurement of defence products.The loan is being raised by the EU through borrowing on capital markets and is backed by the bloc’s budget. Under the arrangement, Ukraine is expected to repay the loan only after it receives war reparations from Russia.Why Ukraine is running short of Patriot missilesKyiv’s request for PAC-3 interceptors comes as Ukraine struggles to maintain adequate stocks of one of its most important air-defence weapons.The Patriot system is among Ukraine’s most capable defences against Russian ballistic missiles, but years of sustained attacks have steadily depleted its interceptor stocks. The problem has become increasingly acute as Moscow has stepped up large-scale long-range missile strikes.The scale of Ukraine’s requirement was highlighted by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in July. He said Ukraine would need at least 140 Patriot interceptors to defend against a single Russian attack involving around 70 ballistic missiles.The challenge is not simply the number of missiles being fired. Russia increasingly combines ballistic missiles with cruise missiles, drones and decoys in complex saturation attacks. This forces Ukrainian air-defence commanders to make difficult decisions about where to deploy a limited supply of high-value interceptors.A further complication is growing global demand for Patriot missiles. The United States used significant numbers of Patriot interceptors during its conflict with Iran, while Gulf countries have also drawn on their own stocks to defend against missile and drone attacks.For Ukraine, the result is a growing race for a weapon that has become indispensable to its defence against Russia’s increasingly sophisticated aerial assault.

articles.title: 'Lost decade of US economy coming': Iran's big warning as tensions flare
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Monday warned the United States of severe economic consequences if Washington targets Iranian e.
articles.body: Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Monday warned the United States of severe economic consequences if Washington targets Iranian energy infrastructure, saying attacks on Iran's oil and gas assets would trigger retaliation against US interests in the region.Ghalibaf issued the warning in a post on X on Monday, as tensions between Tehran and Washington continued to escalate. He pointed to the vulnerability of oil and gas infrastructure across the region and warned that US energy interests could also be exposed to retaliation.“It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed. American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure. Strike our assets and you get struck. We’ve already proven it. Ask the bases that are no longer viable.”Alongside his post, Ghalibaf shared an image featuring oil pipelines in the background and carrying the message: “The lost decade of the US Economy is coming, because some clowns at D.O. [I]. W. decided so.”His remarks came after US secretary of war Pete Hegseth claimed that Iran's oil tanker fleet was vulnerable and warned Tehran against attacking American ships.“It’s simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers. All they have to do is not shoot at @USNavy. Iran’s oil tanker fleet is defenceless — Iran has no navy or air force. Our planes, ships & subs can strike them all in @CENTCOM & @USPACOM.”Hegseth's remarks followed US strikes on Iranian oil tankers, which Washington said were carried out in response to Iranian ballistic missile attacks on US warships.The confrontation has also raised concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies. Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran would keep the waterway open if the US stopped threatening or attacking Iran.“Iran will commit to keeping the Strait of Hormuz open when the US neither threatens nor attacks Iran,” Rezaei told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.Iran has also threatened to establish an “exclusion zone” outside the strait, adding another layer of uncertainty for energy markets and international shipping as tensions continue to mount.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pure selfless love is essence of RSS, not hatred, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat tells London community event
articles.summary: UK News: TOI correspondent from London: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat told community leaders at a reception in Hertfordshire in the UK on Sunday night that “pure sel.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat told community leaders at a reception in Hertfordshire in the UK on Sunday night that “pure selfless love” is the essence of the RSS, not “intense hatred”.When asked what element of the RSS, currently celebrating its centenary, has withstood the test of time, he replied: “If I have to mention a single principle it is ‘apnapan’ (the feeling of oneness, treating everyone as your own). That is ‘Shuddha Saatvika Prem’ (pure and noble love).”Bhagwat was speaking to over 600 community leaders from 326 British diaspora community organisations at the Oshwal Centre in Potters Bar, run by the largest Jain organisation in the UK, the Oshwal Association of the UK, on the third and final leg of his RSS outreach centenary tour.“Hindu is not an individual. He is his family, as well as his community, as well as his society as well as humanity,” Bhagwat said. “So, this ‘apnapan’, this love, is the basis of unity. That is the only one aadhaar (foundation) on which Sangh is built. We sing a song in Sangh. We say: ‘Shuddh saatvik prem apne kaarya ka aadhaar hai (Pure, selfless, and noble love is the very foundation of our work).”The sixth RSS Sarsanghchalak said: “I have heard some people say that intense hatred is the basis of our work. It is just the reverse. ‘Shuddha Saatvika Prem’ is the basis of our work. That is there permanently; it has not worn out even in 100 years. You will find the same 'shuddha saatvika love' in the behaviour of swayamsevaks (volunteer members of the RSS), in the atmosphere of the Sangh," Bhagwat added.His London trip was coordinated by Integral, a UK-based organisation that brings together leaders and communities to strengthen dialogue, collaboration and long-term relationships between the UK and India. Sunday’s event specifically was organised by Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh UK (HSS UK), a Hindu social and cultural organisation established in Britain in 1966, with support from Integral. HSS is separate to and not part of the RSS.Explaining the true meaning of Hindutva, which is heavily misunderstood in the West, Bhagwat said: “The word Hindu, we cannot understand on the basis of any religious practise or lifestyle. Hindu is a nature – a society which has the nature to accept and respect all diversities as it holds that always leads to the same goal.”He translated the famous Sanskrit Shloka in Shiva Mahimna Stotram composed by Pushpadanta, saying: “Due to different tastes, there are different ways, but human beings on those ways have a single destination. Oh God you are that. All the water that falls on earth goes into the sea eventually.”“When we say Hindu is not a religion or worship, there may be Hindu religions. The religions say that all other religions are also true. We have our say, but you have your say, so you are also right. We need not convert each other. You are right and we are right. Because your way is different, we need not be separate, we can live together. Existence is really one. It appears to be diverse. Diversity is natural. We have to accept and respect it and we have to deal with diversity, keeping in mind the differences are various decorations of the unity of existence . One has become many, therefore many are respected. When dealing with them you should not look at them as something separate. All is one, we are one. On this basis we deal with everything.”He also explained the meaning of “Hindu Rashtra”, as it is also commonly misunderstood in the West, saying it does not mean a “nation state.” He said its purpose was to share with the world that diversity is natural and everyone is one and “you can touch happiness”.“It’s a people with one purpose - we should lead a life so that people from all nations look to us and from that derive a way to lead their own life in their own regions with fulfilment, with the purpose of their own nation that is what we mean by ‘rashtra’. Because of the experience of nationalism, there is a fear, but rashtra is not that mission. When this mission progresses, there will never be a dictator or war - it creates peace, bliss, prosperity and brotherhood.”Bhagwat then commented on the political and economic turmoil in the world, saying Hindu civilisational values had the solution. “We think in terms of, we both should get this and, if I get it, I will give some of it to him. If we think like that, we don’t have to conquer nature. We are part of nature. Live and let live and make others live. Hindus have to give this balance to the world. If we give individualism some weight, then we have to keep society away, if we say socialism, then arises the question of individual rights. Society and individuals can progress together and humanity progresses. Hindus have the solution and they can connect and cause the simultaneous progress of anything.”He explained that “seva is nothing which makes you great. Seva is your chance to get nearer to God. You are not doing something good – they are giving immense good to you by giving you the chance to serve. You see God in them and God is giving you a chance to wash your sins by serving them. One should give so that to who we give he also becomes a giver. That type of seva is necessary.”He also said British Hindus should never need to face conflict between their Janmabhumi (land of origin, namely India) and Karmabhumi (land of one’ work and destiny, namely the UK) but if it ever happens, British Hindus will go with the UK. “Hindutva is clear on this: your karmabhumi is where your loyalties lie. Your land of origin is where you get your values and you live those in karmabhumi serving karmabhumi. Hindutva never asks you to betray karmabhumi as you are living there. But your duty is to live your values from Janmabhumi fully and rightly so humanity benefits.”“In Bharat the RSS are working in nearly every walk of life, every aspect and dimension, sports, arts. Farmers, workers, students, women, even politics. We must be self-sufficient but help international trade - that is our ‘swadeshi’. This idea of an organised society should not take 100 years – in the next 20 to 30 years we have to complete,” he concluded.In another development, pro-Khalistan Sikh groups condemned the London gurdwara for hosting him at an event on Friday.The Sikh Federation (UK) (SFUK) said in a statement: “Dozens of gurdwaras, Sikh organisations and individuals have contacted us to express their outrage at the secret visit of Mohan Bhagwat to Khalsa Jatha British Isles Gurdwara. No apology or explanation from those responsible for running the gurdwara, including the trustees can undo the damage caused by welcoming the head of the RSS to a small, private gathering without the presence of the Sangat.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court on Monday termed the Satya Niketan building collapse that killed seven people and injured several others \"most unfortu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court on Monday termed the Satya Niketan building collapse that killed seven people and injured several others "most unfortunate", and questioned not only the responsibility of the building owners but also that of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and Delhi University (DU), which it said had failed to provide adequate accommodation for outstation students dependent on private paying guest (PG) facilities.A bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia directed the authorities to intensify rescue efforts to save those who may still be trapped under the debris.HC flags MCD, DU responsibility in Satya Niketan collapseThe court observed that responsibility for the tragedy did not rest solely with the owners of the collapsed building, news agency PTI reported.It also flagged the role of the MCD and DU, noting that inadequate accommodation facilities force students from outside Delhi to seek shelter in private PGs.The observations were made while hearing a public interest litigation (PIL) concerning the building collapse.Court asks authorities to step up rescue operationsThe bench asked the authorities to "double up the efforts" in the rescue operations so that human lives could be saved.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, Delhi government, Delhi Police and MCD, assured the court that all possible steps were being taken to rescue people trapped under the debris.He said the government was actively monitoring the situation and that some time was needed. Mehta assured the court that the authorities would take all decisions in the interest of everyone concerned and that no stone would be left unturned.Authorities told to file replies within 10 daysThe high court directed the authorities to file their separate replies to the petition within 10 days.The matter has been listed for further hearing on September 25.The PIL was mentioned for an urgent hearing, following which the court agreed to take it up on Monday itself. articles.title: India’s Crude Oil Benchmark Tops $100 as Middle East War Escalates
articles.summary: India’s crude oil benchmark has climbed above $100 per barrel as renewed Middle East fighting drives up oil and shipping costs.
articles.body:
India's average crude import price soared to above $100 per barrel at the end of last week and is set to further rise this week as international crude prices rallied amid intensified hostilities in the Middle East.

The so-called Crude Oil FOB Price, or the Indian Basket of average sweet and sour grades, surged to $101.07 per barrel on Friday, topping the $ 100-a-barrel threshold for the first time since May, data by the Indian Oil Ministry's Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed .

The Indian basket of crude oil is the average of a derived basket comprising a sweet-grade benchmark, Dated Brent, and the sour-grade benchmark of the Oman and Dubai average imported by Indian refineries during each month.

As of Monday, the average Indian Basket of crude oil so far in September was $99.38 per barrel, up from $83 in June, $82 in July, and $90 in August.

The average hit $100 in early September, as international crude oil prices rallied amid the re-escalation in the Middle East, as the United States and Iran continue to exchange strikes and fire for more than a week now.

India's crude oil import bill has soared in recent months, due to the reduced oil flows from the Middle East and the high risks to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The freight rates on the key route from Ras Tanura on Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf to India have soared by more than 400% since February 28, when the war began and Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz.

India paid 60% more for crude oil imports in the April-June quarter compared to the same period last year, as the surge in oil prices offset slightly lower import volumes.

The rise continued into the beginning of the third quarter, with the July import bill 41% higher than a year earlier.

articles.title: In 2018, a family bought a 1906 train car for $3,000 after finding 20 feral cats inside; then spent $147,000 restoring it as an Airbnb
articles.summary: US News: In 2018, an old wooden railway carriage was hiding beneath a farm shed in Idaho, so neglected that it was difficult to tell what it had once been. Its.
articles.body: In 2018, an old wooden railway carriage was hiding beneath a farm shed in Idaho, so neglected that it was difficult to tell what it had once been. Its windows were broken, the timber was deteriorating and around 20 feral cats had moved in. Then Isaac French’s father noticed faded paint and the numbers 306, offering a clue to its past. Built in 1906, the 61-foot carriage had spent decades away from the railway, eventually being used to store grain and feed cattle. A post shared on Instagram by a US couple reveals how the wooden railway carriage was transformed from a neglected farm storage space into a $350-a-night holiday rental.The family bought it for $3,000, but getting it home took another two years. What followed was an extensive restoration, carried out largely by the family, costing about $147,000. By August 2020, the neglected carriage had been transformed into a holiday rental, where guests can now stay for more than $350 a night.What looked like farm storage in 2018 had a railway pastThis began in December 2018, when Isaac French's father was helping an elderly neighbour clear snow from a barn. On the property stood a long, open-sided agricultural shed, and beneath it was something that appeared to have been abandoned for years.According to People.com, it was a wooden railway carriage, though its condition made that difficult to recognise at first. The windows were damaged, the sills had rotted and dirt covered much of what remained. There was another complication inside: about 20 feral cats had taken over the carriage.French's father, however, knew enough about the local railway history to look more closely. Near the passenger section, traces of old paint could still be seen. Beside the broken clerestory windows were the faint numbers 3, 0 and 6.Those details led the family to identify it as Washington, Idaho & Montana Railway Car 306, a carriage manufactured by the American Car & Foundry Company in St Charles, Missouri, in 1906.The discovery changed the way they looked at the battered old structure. Rather than being an unidentifiable farm building, it was a surviving piece of local railway history.After leaving the rails in the 1950s, Car 306 found a new life on a farmCar 306 had not been sitting beneath that shed since its railway days. According to French, it arrived on the farm sometime in the 1950s, after the tracks in the area were removed.A previous owner had acquired the carriage as scrap and transported it roughly 10 miles to the property. There, its purpose changed completely. The former railway car became agricultural storage, eventually helping with jobs around the farm such as storing grain and feeding cattle.That long period of neglect left plenty to deal with. The family found an exterior battered by years of exposure and an interior that had accumulated layers of grime. The cats had made themselves comfortable inside, too. French later joked that the first thing his father encountered when approaching the carriage was not its history but its smell.Yet the shed that had hidden the carriage away for so long had also done something unexpected. It had protected much of the original structure.The 61-foot train car finally moved in 2020The French family agreed to buy Car 306 for $3,000. The deal was simple enough: a handshake followed by a cheque.For two years, the family tried to find someone capable of moving a 61-foot wooden railway car in poor condition. Several movers declined after seeing what was involved. The size alone was awkward, and transporting an old timber carriage over rural roads presented its own problems. Eventually, someone agreed to take it on.The move happened in February 2020, on a cold, wet day. A semi-truck hauled the carriage along icy, winding back roads for about three hours. When the route reached the final hill towards the French family's property, the truck could not manage the climb on its own.A bulldozer was brought in and pushed from the front. Only then did Car 306 finally reach the place where its next life would begin.The 2020 restoration turned into a $147,000 family projectBefore serious restoration could begin, the carriage needed protection from the weather.French had drawn up plans for a timber-framed structure inspired by traditional railway depot architecture. His brothers constructed the roof over the carriage, creating a sheltered space where the restoration could continue without leaving the old timber exposed to Idaho's conditions. The timing made the job considerably harder.Reportedly, renovation work began in January 2020. Within weeks, the pandemic had disrupted normal life and created problems with materials, money and construction work. The family had originally paid just $3,000 for the carriage, but restoring it properly was becoming a much larger undertaking.The eventual restoration cost about $147,000. Much of the work was done by the family themselves, which helped keep the figure from rising further. French's father and brothers handled plumbing and electrical work. French took on sanding, epoxy repairs, brasswork and the lettering. A friend made a copper chandelier by hand, while his mother searched for antiques to furnish the finished interior.It became a family construction project as much as a preservation job.A century-old photograph helped restore Car 306One of the most useful things the family had was not a modern plan or a set of restoration drawings.It was a photograph. A picture of Car 306 from around the time it was built in 1906 showed the family what the original carriage had looked like. That mattered because they were not trying to create a generic railway-themed accommodation. They could use the surviving photograph to work out details that had disappeared during decades of agricultural use.The original timber proved surprisingly resilient. Much of it could remain in place, while sections around damaged window sills were repaired with epoxy.The brass fittings were cleaned and restored. The windows were repaired. The faded gold lettering was recreated.Some of these jobs took far longer than their finished appearance might suggest. A restored letter or polished brass fitting can seem like a small detail once everything is complete. During the restoration, though, each one represented another piece of work standing between the family and the finished carriage.The railway layout became part of the accommodationWhen Car 306 was finally completed in August 2020, the family had found a way to give its old spaces new purposes without simply stripping out the interior.The former mail compartment became the main bedroom.The cargo area was converted into a bathroom, while the passenger section became a reading lounge. A small kitchenette was fitted into the existing woodwork so that it did not dominate the carriage's original character.There is also a gas-powered potbelly stove in the lounge.The result is not simply an old carriage with modern rooms installed inside it. Much of the original structure remains visible, with the restored wood, windows, brass and lettering providing the setting for the new accommodation.From farm storage to a $350-a-night stayThe finished Car 306 is now offered as an Airbnb in Deary, Idaho. Guests can stay inside a railway carriage that was built more than a century ago and spent much of its later life doing something far removed from passenger travel.The nightly rate is now more than $350, and French says the property is booked roughly 90 per cent of the time. By his account, the rental recovered the restoration costs within about its first year.But the family says the accommodation was not the original reason for buying the carriage. The idea came later, after they had already decided that the old railway car was worth saving.That sequence is important to how French describes the project. They did not begin with a plan to purchase an unusual building and turn it into a holiday rental. They encountered an old carriage that was close to disappearing and eventually found that hospitality provided a practical way to preserve it.Car 306 now offers guests a stay inside railway historyFor French, one of the quieter pleasures of the restored carriage is the reading lounge.He has described sitting in a comfortable chair with a book, looking through the windows towards the hills and pine trees outside. The setting is not identical to the railway journeys Car 306 made more than a century ago, of course, but the landscape still provides a link with its working life.The farm shed that made it look abandoned and useless also protected the wood from the elements. The agricultural conversion that removed it from railway service may have helped keep the original structure intact long enough for someone to recognise what it was.Today, visitors pay to spend a night inside that same structure.The 20 cats are gone, the grain is gone and the carriage no longer sits beneath a farm shed. But the timber, brasswork, lettering and proportions of Car 306 remain, giving the old railway vehicle a new purpose without entirely erasing the one it had before.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A British house was built with old duvets inside its walls and oyster shells on its exterior to show how everyday waste could be reused in construction
articles.summary: UK News: A house in Brighton was built with some unlikely materials hidden in plain sight. Inside its walls were old duvets and discarded bedding, reused as in.
articles.body: A house in Brighton was built with some unlikely materials hidden in plain sight. Inside its walls were old duvets and discarded bedding, reused as insulation rather than sent to landfill. On the outside, oyster shells collected from a local restaurant were turned into experimental tiles designed to protect that insulation from the weather. The project was developed at the Brighton Waste House by researchers from the University of Brighton with Local Works Studio, as part of a wider attempt to find uses for waste generated close to construction sites.According to researchers at the University of Brighton, the restaurant supplying the shells discarded more than 50,000 of them each year, giving the researchers a plentiful material to work with. Some shells were used directly, while others were heated at around 900°C to make quicklime before being combined with crushed shell. The mixture was moulded and left to harden, producing tiles that became part of the building's exterior.How did researchers turn discarded oyster shells into building tilesThe University of Brighton team developed the tiles as part of a project exploring how waste materials could be reused in construction. The tiles were designed to remain on the outer surface of the Brighton Waste House, protecting insulation made from reused bedding and duvets. The project brought together the university team and Local Works Studio, a specialist working on material development. The oyster shells came from English’s restaurant in Brighton, which supplied shells that would otherwise have been discarded. The research record says the restaurant threw away more than 50,000 shells each year. Construction waste from the Preston Barracks development was also incorporated into the project, bringing together two different waste streams to create a new building material.The shells were prepared in different ways before being used as tiles. Some were used directly, while others were heated to create quick lime. The project record describes shells being burnt at about 900 degrees before being combined with crushed oyster shells, which acted as aggregate. The mixture was then pressed into silicone moulds and left for several days. After adding water, the mixture underwent a natural chemical reaction that made it hard. The resulting pieces were described as concrete tiles and were made using a process similar to traditional Roman concrete.Why were oyster shells considered for constructionOyster shells are made up of more than 90% calcium carbonate, a material widely used in cement production. As part of the INTERREG SB&WRC programme, researchers explored whether waste materials found near construction sites could be reused for insulation and rain-screen external wall coverings in social housing. The idea was to keep local waste within the building process rather than simply discarding it. This was particularly relevant to shells, with the exhibition catalogue noting that the seafood industry discards millions of tonnes of them each year.How a Brighton project turned oyster waste into a building prototypeThe oyster-shell tiles reached an audience beyond Brighton. Samples were exhibited in Adelaide, South Australia, in 2018 as part of an exhibition linked to the ‘Unmaking Waste conference’. The event brought attention to the project’s attempt to connect waste, design and construction through a prototype. The Brighton work was led by Duncan Baker-Brown with Nick Gant, alongside collaborators including Local Works Studio. The focus was on creating an unusual tile and showing how discarded materials could be given another role within buildings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Argentina planted eucalyptus across grassland; scientists found the trees were pulling groundwater down by more than half a metre
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A stand of eucalyptus trees planted in Argentina’s vast ‘Pampas grasslands’ was found to be reshaping the water beneath its roots. A study titled ‘Hyd.
articles.body: A stand of eucalyptus trees planted in Argentina’s vast ‘Pampas grasslands’ was found to be reshaping the water beneath its roots. A study titled ‘Hydrological consequences of Eucalyptus afforestation in the Argentine Pampas’ examined how a 40-hectare plantation of ‘Eucalyptus camaldulensis’ affected local groundwater compared with the surrounding native grassland. Scientists found that the trees used water at rates of up to 3.7 millimetres per day, drawing enough from below the surface to lower the groundwater level by more than half a metre. As the water table beneath the plantation fell, groundwater from the surrounding grassland began moving towards the trees. The study also showed that the eucalyptus changed its water sources with the seasons, relying more heavily on deep groundwater when the upper soil layers became dry. The findings reveal how replacing grassland with deep-rooted trees can alter an entire local water system.How did eucalyptus trees in Argentina pull groundwater down by more than half a metreThe research focused on a 40-hectare plantation near Castelli in the Flooding Pampas of central Argentina. According to the study, the plantation had been established in 1951 and was surrounded by native grassland. The researchers monitored the site for two years, combining measurements of water moving through the trees with groundwater levels and soil moisture. Their results showed that the eucalyptus plantation released water through its leaves, at an average rate of about 2 millimetres per day, reaching peaks of approximately 3.7 millimetres.That demand for water had a clear effect underground. The study found that groundwater levels beneath the plantation were more than ‘0.5 metres lower’ than those in the surrounding grassland. The difference created an underground gradient that encouraged water to move horizontally from the grassland towards the plantation. In other words, the trees were not simply using the water already beneath them. Their water use was also drawing groundwater in from the neighbouring landscape. At night, when transpiration slowed, groundwater beneath the plantation could rise again as water flowed into the area.The eucalyptus switched their water source when the soil dried upThe eucalyptus trees did not rely on a single source of water throughout the year. According to the study, the trees used moisture stored in the unsaturated upper layers of soil as well as deeper groundwater. When the upper soil was relatively wet, that soil moisture could provide a substantial share of the water used by the trees. Conditions changed as the summer became drier. As surface soil moisture declined, the trees increasingly depended on water from below the water table. During the driest periods, the researchers found that Eucalyptus behaved almost entirely as a groundwater-dependent species.The change was especially important because the trees could continue accessing deep water even when the upper layers of soil had dried out. Native grasses, by contrast, generally had much shallower root systems. The study reported that grassland roots typically extended to around 1 to 2 metres, while roots in the eucalyptus plantation reached depths of about 5 to 6 metres. That difference gave the trees access to water beyond the reach of much of the surrounding vegetation.The study suggested that roughly 67% of the water used by the eucalyptus trees over a year came directly from groundwater. The researchers estimated that direct groundwater uptake through the roots amounted to approximately 395 millimetres per year. The remaining water came largely from moisture held in the soil, with rainfall also contributing to the overall water system. The study found that precipitation and groundwater flowing in from the surrounding grassland were both major inputs to the plantation.How did the deep water table redirect groundwater towards the eucalyptusMeasurements showed that the difference in groundwater levels between the grassland and plantation ranged from around 0.2 to 0.6 metres. This meant that the eucalyptus plantation effectively became an area towards which groundwater flowed. Water moved from the shallower water table beneath the grassland towards the deeper water table beneath the trees. The researchers also observed daily fluctuations in groundwater beneath the plantation of up to 15 centimetres during periods of high water use. Groundwater levels fell during the day as the trees drew water through their roots and rose at night as water moved back into the plantation area.The findings show how afforestation can reshape grassland hydrologyThe study’s broader message concerns what happens when deep-rooted trees replace naturally treeless grasslands. The Pampas are extremely flat, and groundwater lies relatively close to the surface across much of the region. Under these conditions, a plantation capable of reaching and using groundwater can alter the normal movement of water through the landscape. The researchers concluded that large-scale eucalyptus planting could produce seasonal changes in groundwater levels and surface soil moisture compared with conditions under native grassland. Water tables may also remain low for longer after dry periods because the trees continue drawing heavily on groundwater.The findings do not suggest that every eucalyptus plantation will produce identical effects. Soil conditions, rainfall and the movement of groundwater can all influence the outcome. Yet the Castelli plantation offered a striking example that when land use changes above the surface, some of its most significant consequences may be unfolding silently beneath it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi building collapse: Rahul demands accountability, accuses PM Modi & BJP of grandstanding
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha LoP and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday and the BJP government over th.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha LoP and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday and the BJP government over the collapse of a PG building in Delhi’s Satya Niketan, accusing the government of failing to prevent such accidents and holding those responsible accountable.In a post on X, Gandhi accused that the BJP government follows a pattern of taking no preventive action before accidents and then “grandstanding” after tragedies, while blaming a few lower-level officials and allowing those he described as the “real culprits” to escape accountability.Gandhi said the Satya Niketan collapse was “no isolated tragedy” and referred to other recent incidents in Delhi, including deaths in Saidulajab and a fire in Hauz Rani. He alleged that lives and aspirations were repeatedly being lost in such incidents while meaningful action remained absent.“Every time, lives, dreams, and aspirations get buried under rubble, and every time, any real action is nowhere to be found,” Rahul said.The Congress leader also accused the Prime Minister of attempting to shame and silence those who question the government by using labels such as “dimagi naxal” and “naraz fufa”. He said the alleged lack of accountability was a consequence of a lack of political intent.“For 12 years, this government has spun you around with lofty talk about the whole world, but never addressed the real issues,” Gandhi said, questioning the BJP government's record on public safety.He also raised questions over governance in Delhi, saying the city has a “triple engine” government and asking what the excuse was for the administration's alleged helplessness in dealing with recurring safety failures.Satya Niketan PG building collapsed during repair workThe building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, housed a boys' paying-guest accommodation.It collapsed on Sunday while repair work was underway, leaving seven people dead and several others injured.The Delhi high court on Monday termed the Satya Niketan building collapse as "most unfortunate", and questioned not only the responsibility of the building owners but also that of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and Delhi University (DU), which it said had failed to provide adequate accommodation for outstation students dependent on private paying guest (PG) facilities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body:
Several people have been killed in Russia and Crimea in Ukrainian counterattacks, including one person in Perm and two in Crimea, with multiple buildings damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Ukrainian attacks on targets in Russia, including refineries in Ryazan, Perm, and Tatarstan, as well as in Kursk region and the Black Sea.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a Russian invasion for over four and a half years, leading to repeated attacks on Russian targets, including in Crimea, which Russia uses as a staging area and supply base.

Several people have been killed in Russia and on the Black Sea peninsula of Crimea annexed by Russia in Ukrainian counterattacks, Russian authorities said on Monday.

In Perm, more than 1,100 kilometres east of Moscow, one person was killed as a result of a Ukrainian attack, regional governor Dmitri Machonin said.

Four others were injured and a multi-storey residential building was damaged, he added. Machonin spoke of a massive attack in which 27 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over the Perm region.

In the border region of Belgorod, a man was killed in the town of Grayvoron in a Ukrainian drone attack, according to the regional civil defence authority. A woman was injured, it said. Another person was injured in further attacks and there was damage and fires, according to the information.

Moscow-appointed authorities: Two dead in Crimea

On the Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014, the Moscow-appointed governor of the city of Sevastopol, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said a man and a teenage girl had been killed in a Ukrainian attack. Eight multi-storey residential buildings were damaged, he said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Ukrainian attacks on targets in Russia. A refinery in Ryazan region was damaged, he said. Refineries in Perm region and the Republic of Tatarstan were also targeted, he said. Targets in Kursk region and in the Black Sea were also attacked, he added.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a Russian invasion for more than four and a half years. As part of its defensive fight, it repeatedly also targets sites in the Russian hinterland. Russia uses Crimea as a staging area and supply base. Kiev therefore also repeatedly attacks there.

articles.title: Panama Canal warns of cutting 5 ship transits a day, adding to global shipping woes
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a further potential addition to global shipping woes, the Panama Canal may reduce the number of ships allowed to transit the waterway to as few as .
articles.body: In a further potential addition to global shipping woes, the Panama Canal may reduce the number of ships allowed to transit the waterway to as few as 27 a day in the coming months due to worsening water shortages.The Panama Canal Authority has modelled the potential reduction as a “worst-case scenario” based on rainfall patterns recorded in 1997, the canal’s driest year on record, reported Financial Times. The canal currently allows about 32 daily transits, down from its usual average of 36, after water shortages forced authorities to restrict traffic.“[Climate change is] the most important thing because, I mean, we can see how the frequency of dry years is increasing,” Espino de Marotta said, warning that water shortages were becoming a problem “every three years or so”, its new administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta told FT.The canal, which connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and handles more than 3 per cent of global trade, relies on freshwater reservoirs to operate its locks. Authorities have introduced water-saving measures and reduced transits to preserve supplies ahead of the dry season from December to mid-April.The restrictions come as global shipping is already facing disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East and traffic constraints around the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping costs for Panama Canal transits have surged, with average auction costs for standard and larger locks rising from $66,150 and $253,180 in January-February to $478,750 and $1.25 million, respectively.“The Panama Canal is a wild card in the world of commodity movements and trade patterns,” said Kristian Sørensen, chief executive of BW LPG.The potential cuts could put further pressure on global trade and commodity flows, with shipping companies already rerouting vessels on longer journeys around Africa or South America.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
